claims.text: Controlled rolling followed by short subtransus annealing will generate a bimodal microstructure in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The resulting bimodal microstructure will contain fine, uniformly distributed ductile precipitates within a primary high-strength refractory matrix.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment will improve tensile ductility and uniform deformability relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed treatment will not cause a marked loss of yield strength.
The proposed treatment will not reduce impact-induced energy release under high-strain-rate loading.
As-cast or as-solidified Mo-, Nb-, Ta-, and W-based refractory high-entropy alloys typically exhibit limited ductility and localized deformation.
Rolling introduces defects and stored deformation energy into the alloy.
A subsequent short anneal uses the stored energy to drive partial recrystallization.
A subsequent short anneal will drive controlled precipitation of a secondary, more ductile phase.
Fine ductile precipitates and the engineered grain-boundary network will distribute strain more uniformly and reduce strain localization.
The dominant refractory phase will preserve high strength after processing.
The dominant refractory phase will preserve the alloy's capacity for impact-induced energy release.
Annealing at approximately 1150–1200 °C for a calibrated duration can produce the desired bimodal microstructure.
The untreated cast or conventionally processed baseline typically has a coarse, monolithic microstructure.
The hypothesis should apply to refractory high-entropy alloys having compositions and phase stabilities similar to MoNbTaW-based systems.
Excessive grain growth or precipitate coarsening could compromise strength.
